title: The process model and the project lifecycle
blurb: Place the seven PRINCE2 processes on the project lifecycle and say which management level runs each one.
question: A project has three stages. Which processes are used in the final stage, and is managing a stage boundary run at its end?

teach.body: Formally: the seven PRINCE2 processes provide the set of activities needed to direct, manage and deliver a project successfully. In plain English: the processes say who does what, and when, from the first idea to the final handover. Each process belongs to a management level (directing, managing or delivering) and is used at a particular point in the project lifecycle.

teach.h: A three-stage project on a timeline

teach.body: First, there are at least two management stages, and the first is always the initiation stage. Second, managing a stage boundary is first used at the end of initiation and then at the end of each later stage except the final one; it can also prepare an exception plan at any time, even in the final stage. Third, closing a project is not a stage: it is the last part of the final stage.

teach.h: What each process chapter tells you
items: Purpose (x.1) and objectives (x.2): why the process exists and what it must achieve.
Context (x.3): its trigger, where it sits and how it links to other processes.
Activities (x.4), with recommended actions for each.
Tailoring (x.5), responsibilities as a RACI table (x.6) and how the practices are applied (x.7).

teach.body: Calderbrook Council wants to refit its central library. The business layer issues a mandate, and project manager Tomasz Wilk runs starting up a project. Executive Grace Osei's board authorizes initiation, and Tomasz runs initiating a project in stage 1, then managing a stage boundary. In stage 2 he controls the stage while contractor team manager Lena Varga runs managing product delivery. Stage 3 ends with closing a project inside the stage, with no further stage boundary.

teach.text: Classic traps: closing a project is NOT its own stage, and managing a stage boundary is NOT used at the end of the final stage (only to prepare an exception plan if one is needed). Starting up a project is pre-project, so it is not a stage either. The first stage is initiation.

items: Seven processes: SU, DP, IP, CS, MP, SB, CP.
Directing = DP (board); managing = SU, IP, CS, SB, CP (PM); delivering = MP (team managers). SU spans directing and managing.
Lifecycle: pre-project (SU), initiation stage (IP, SB), later stages (CS, MP, SB), final stage (CS, MP, CP).
At least two stages; initiation is first; closing sits inside the final stage.
DP runs from the request to initiate until after closing a project.

summary: You can now name the seven processes, say which management level runs each one and place them on the lifecycle from pre-project to the final stage. You can also apply the rules on stage boundaries, closure and the minimum of two stages.

A.q: Which process is used by the directing level from the end of starting up a project until the project closes?
A.why: Directing a project is the project board's process. It begins with the request to initiate and continues until after closing a project (manual 12, fig 12.1).

whyNot.0: Controlling a stage is the project manager's day-to-day process during a stage, at the managing level.
whyNot.1: Managing a stage boundary is a managing-level process used near the end of each stage except the final one.
whyNot.3: Closing a project is a managing-level process at the end of the final stage.

A.q: Which process is carried out by team managers at the delivering level?
A.why: Managing product delivery is the delivering-level process, used by team managers to accept, execute and deliver work packages.

whyNot.1: Controlling a stage is the project manager's process for assigning and monitoring work.
whyNot.2: Initiating a project is run by the project manager during the initiation stage.
whyNot.3: Managing a stage boundary is run by the project manager near the end of a stage.

A.q: In which part of the project lifecycle does starting up a project take place?
A.why: Starting up a project happens before the project formally exists: it is pre-project, ahead of the initiation stage.

whyNot.0: Initiation is the first stage of the project and uses initiating a project, which follows starting up.
whyNot.1: Delivery stages come after initiation and use controlling a stage and managing product delivery.
whyNot.2: The final stage contains closing a project, not starting up.

B.q:
Which two statements about managing a stage boundary are correct?
1. It is first used at the end of the initiation stage.
2. It is used at the end of the final stage to plan closure.
3. It can be used to prepare an exception plan in the final stage.
4. It is used before initiation to plan the initiation stage.
B.why: Managing a stage boundary is first used at the end of initiation (1) and can prepare an exception plan at any time, including the final stage (3).

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is false: managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage; closure is planned in the final stage plan.
whyNot.2: Statements 2 and 4 are both false: there is no boundary after the final stage, and the initiation stage plan is made in starting up a project.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: the initiation stage is planned in starting up a project, not managing a stage boundary.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. A PRINCE2 project has at least two management stages, the first of which is the [?] stage.
B.why: There must be at least two stages, and the first is always the initiation stage (manual 12, fig 12.1).

whyNot.0: Delivery stages follow the initiation stage; at least one is needed, but it is not the first.
whyNot.1: Pre-project is the period before the project's stages, when starting up a project runs.
whyNot.2: Starting up a project is a pre-project process, not a management stage.

B.q: Which statement about closing a project is correct?
options: It is a separate stage after the final stage
It is the last part of the final stage
It follows a final stage boundary review
It is run by the board in its own process
B.why: Closing a project is not a stage; it is carried out as the last part of the final stage and is planned in the final stage plan.

whyNot.0: Closure is never planned as a stage of its own; it sits inside the final stage.
whyNot.2: Managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage, so no boundary review precedes closure.
whyNot.3: Closing a project is run by the project manager; the board's part is authorizing closure in directing a project.

C.q: During a delivery stage that is not the final stage, which two processes does the project manager use?
options: Controlling a stage and managing a stage boundary
Controlling a stage and managing product delivery
Initiating a project and managing a stage boundary
Directing a project and controlling a stage
C.why: In a later delivery stage the PM controls the stage day to day, then uses managing a stage boundary as the stage nears its end.

whyNot.1: Managing product delivery is used in delivery stages, but by team managers, not the project manager.
whyNot.2: Initiating a project is used only in the initiation stage, so it is not part of a delivery stage.
whyNot.3: Directing a project is the project board's process, not the project manager's.

C.q: Which process continues from the end of starting up a project until after closing a project, and at which level is it used?
options: Controlling a stage, at the managing level
Managing a stage boundary, at the directing level
Directing a project, at the directing level
Directing a project, at the managing level
C.why: Directing a project spans the whole project from the request to initiate to authorizing closure, and it is the project board's directing-level process.

whyNot.0: Controlling a stage runs within each delivery stage, not across the whole project.
whyNot.1: Managing a stage boundary is a managing-level process used near stage ends.
whyNot.3: The process is right, but it belongs to the directing level (the board), not the managing level.

C.q: A project has three stages. In which stage is closing a project carried out, and is a stage boundary managed at the end of that stage?
options: In stage 3, with no boundary at its end
In a fourth stage added for closure
In stage 3, followed by a stage boundary
C.why: Closing a project is the last part of the final stage (stage 3 here), and managing a stage boundary is not used at the end of the final stage.

whyNot.1: Closure is never planned as a stage of its own, so no fourth stage is added.
whyNot.2: Stage 3 is right, but no stage boundary is managed at the end of the final stage.
whyNot.3: Closing a project happens at the end of the final stage, which here is stage 3, not stage 2.

reteach.title: Who acts, and when
reteach.question: If you only remember one picture of the process model, what should it show?

blocks.h: Board decides, manager manages, teams build
blocks.body: The project board directs through one process: directing a project. The project manager runs five: starting up (with the executive), initiating, controlling a stage, managing a stage boundary and closing. Team managers run one: managing product delivery. Then add time: starting up is pre-project, initiation is stage 1, later stages deliver, and the final stage ends with closing.

items.label: Initiating a project, then a stage boundary
Controlling a stage, managing product delivery, stage boundary
Controlling a stage, managing product delivery, closing a project

blocks.text: Count the stage plans, not the processes: the initiation stage is planned in starting up a project, every other stage in managing a stage boundary, and there is no boundary after the final stage.

explain.body: Directing: directing a project (the board). Managing: starting up, initiating, controlling a stage, managing a stage boundary and closing (the project manager). Delivering: managing product delivery (team managers). Starting up a project also involves the directing level, because the business layer and executive make the key appointments.

test.q: Which level of management uses initiating a project?
test.why: Initiating a project is run by the project manager, at the managing level.

whyNot.0: The directing level (the board) uses directing a project and authorizes the outcome of initiation.
whyNot.2: The delivering level uses managing product delivery, which starts in the delivery stages.
whyNot.3: The business layer sits outside the project and provides the mandate; it does not run initiation.

explain.body: Pre-project: starting up a project. Initiation stage: initiating a project, then managing a stage boundary. Later delivery stages: controlling a stage and managing product delivery, then a stage boundary. Final stage: controlling a stage, managing product delivery and closing a project.

test.q: Which process is used before the project's first stage begins?
test.why: Starting up a project is pre-project: it decides whether initiation is worthwhile before the initiation stage begins.

whyNot.0: Initiating a project is the work of the first stage, the initiation stage.
whyNot.1: Directing a project begins when starting up a project requests initiation, so it is not the pre-project process.
whyNot.3: Managing a stage boundary is first used at the end of the initiation stage.

explain.body: Managing a stage boundary is first used at the end of initiation, then at the end of each later stage except the final one. It also prepares exception plans whenever the board asks, including in the final stage. Closing a project is part of the final stage, not a stage.

explain.h: Is a stage boundary managed here?

test.q: When is managing a stage boundary first used?
options: At the end of the first delivery stage
At the end of the final stage
At the end of the initiation stage
test.why: Managing a stage boundary is first used near the end of the initiation stage, to plan the first delivery stage.

whyNot.0: Before initiation the project is still in starting up a project, which plans the initiation stage.
whyNot.1: It is used at the end of delivery stages too, but the first use is at the end of initiation.
whyNot.2: It is not used at the end of the final stage, where closing a project takes place.

explain.body: Directing a project starts when starting up a project sends the request to initiate and runs until after closing a project, when the board authorizes closure. In between, the board makes its decisions at key points and gives ongoing direction, without managing day to day.

test.q: What triggers the start of directing a project?
options: The project mandate from the business
The executive's approval of the brief
The initiation notice from the board
test.why: Directing a project starts on the request to initiate a project, which ends starting up a project.

whyNot.0: The project mandate triggers starting up a project, not directing a project.
whyNot.2: Approving the project brief is part of the board's first DP activity, so it cannot be the trigger.
whyNot.3: The initiation notice is an output of authorize initiation, issued after DP has started.
